title: Under the Arch
part: PART ONE: SIXTY-ONE CHIMNEYS AND ONE TROLL

pages.text:
*From the Bridgewater Almanac: Never go under the old bridge. There is nothing there but damp.*

Rue descended the mossy steps. The air under the arch did not smell of damp. It smelled of woodsmoke, old paper, and something sweet, like dried apples. It was a room, curved and high, with a tiny iron stove glowing red in the corner. A kettle sat on top, humming a low, steady note. Shelves of books were wedged into the stone walls, and on the floor, a garden of moss grew in careful, swirling patterns.

In the center of it all sat a troll.

He was the size of a haystack, grey-green and mossy, perched on an upturned wooden bucket. His hand rested on his cheek. He wore round spectacles mended with twine and a waistcoat with a great many pockets. Two small, blunt tusks jutted from his lower lip.

He looked up.

Rue opened her mouth. The troll opened his.

They both screamed, politely and in unison, because the almanac had never explained what to do if the monster was crying.
pages.image: A cozy curved stone room under a bridge with a glowing stove and shelves of books; a large mossy troll with twine-mended spectacles sits on a bucket holding his cheek while a small freckled girl in a yellow coat screams at him.

pages.text:
The troll stopped screaming first. He lowered his hand, looked at Rue, and then looked at the bucket.

"Please don't tell anyone," he said. His voice was like gravel rolling in a box. "I'll leave. I'm very good at leaving. It is a talent I have honed over three centuries."

He shifted on the bucket, wincing. "Only the lantern's broken. And I can't see the stones to fix the bridge. And I have a tooth."

"I have a name," he added, rubbing his ear, which looked like a large, green leaf. "It is Hobb."

"I am Rue," she said, because he had introduced himself, and it seemed rude not to.

Hobb nodded. He apologized. Then he apologized again for the noise. He apologized for the teeth. He apologized for the moss, which had gotten a little too ambitious near the stove. He apologized for the fact that he was there at all. He apologized six times in three minutes, and Rue found her feet shuffling back and forth, feeling like a fly on a plate.
pages.image: The mossy troll Hobb sits on a wooden bucket, rubbing his ear and looking embarrassed, while Rue stands stiffly in her yellow raincoat, holding her hands at her sides in a small stone room.

pages.text:
"Where does it hurt?" Rue asked.

Hobb blinked behind his round spectacles, looking as if he had just heard a question he did not know how to answer. "The back, left side. The tusk-tooth. It throbs like a drum in a barrel, which is very undignified."

Rue had never once in her life walked past a person with a toothache, but she knew exactly what Gran did for that sort of thing. She knew about clove oil wrapped in cotton, and the little salt water rinse, and the need for silence because throbbing teeth do not appreciate loud conversation.

"It will pass," Rue said, though she knew it would not. Not on its own. "I will be back tomorrow with the oil."

Hobb looked at her. His broad, kind face seemed to fold in on itself, confused and hopeful at the same time. "You will? Most people do not come back. They run, or they throw things. Usually both."

"I brought scones," Rue said, which was not true, but it was a nice thought. "I will bring oil. Right then."
pages.image: Rue stands facing the large troll, who looks surprised and hopeful, his hand still near his cheek; the background shows the swirling moss garden and the glowing stove, creating a warm, intimate atmosphere.

pages.text:
"You are the first person in a long time to offer a solution," Hobb said, scratching his head with one thick finger. "The others offer stones. Or silence. Occasionally, a very aggressive poem."

He looked around the room. "I have a toll, you know. For crossing the bridge. It is the oldest rule. Nobody pays it in a long time. They just walk across, or don't. But the toll is... one story. From anyone who wants to cross. I like stories. I am very bad at making them, but I like hearing them."

Rue considered this. She had plenty of stories. She had a story about Biscuit, the Kettle & Crumb’s cat, who had stolen a kipper off the Mayor’s plate last Tuesday and then spent the afternoon pretending to be a statue by the window.

Hobb listened. He did not laugh until the end, when Rue described the Mayor’s face. Then he laughed. It was a low, rumbling sound, like a cello being played by a giant. The kettle on the stove jumped, and a puff of steam shot out like a surprised snake.
pages.image: Hobb leans forward, laughing heartily, while Rue smiles shyly, her hands clasped; the iron kettle on the stove behind them is steaming vigorously, and the moss on the floor ripples slightly from the vibration of his laughter.

pages.text:
Rue climbed the mossy steps. The dusk had turned to night. The air was cool and smelled of wet stone. She reached the top of the bridge and looked out over the river. The town lights were on, yellow and steady. The Bridge Club had gone home. Nobody had seen her.

She stood there for a long time. The water lapped against the arch below. She told herself the truth, because she was good at getting things right. She had a secret. And she had a friend. In that order. She was not sure she had ever had either before today.

"Right then," she said to the river, because it was a good time to say it.

She turned and walked home. She had to steal clove oil. And she had to be very, very good at it.
pages.image: Rue stands on the old stone bridge at night, looking out at the glowing town lights across the river; her yellow raincoat stands out against the dark stone, and she looks small but resolute against the large, mossy arch below her.
